semantics.diagram_cases: Real Grilling page questions from vstack and Tern pages. context and option are the labels gpt-6.1-sol gave at high thinking. Each case's probabilities sat at least 0.1 from the thresholds when chosen, so judge noise does not flip it. A case passes when each kind's probability is at or over its threshold exactly when its label is true.
semantics.type_cases: One hand-written question per figure kind. expected names the Pele Mermaid type that draws it best, and allowed names other types that draw it well. A case passes when expected, or a type in allowed, is among the top types of context_type or option_type, in the request that grilling-page's helper sends through judge_batch. scripts/visual_judge_check.py runs every case in omp's Python eval.

state.title: How does a vstack skill row reach implement when the session's checkout is not a vstack clone?
state.description:
session-lessons can run in any project. A finding about a vstack skill then points into a vstack clone, which is a different repo than the session's checkout. Today session-lessons runs vstack-edit from the root of that clone. Now the vstack-maintain Addon tells implement what to run, and implement works in a worktree when the checkout is the live plugin ([How does the merged Addon for Updates and Hand edits work?](https://github.com/daandden/vstack/issues/124)).

implement keeps one run record with one current branch and one End state. This choice decides whether one implement run can span two repos.

session checkout:  ~/work/shop          (finding about shop/.omp/skills/x)
vstack clone:      ~/work/tries/vstack  (finding about plugin/skills/tdd)

session-lessons step 4 reads principle-encode-lessons-in-structure and moves an Accepted item that a lint, script, metadata flag, or runtime check enforces better to Backlog. correct's ladder ranks the same choice: architecture, then types, then a lint whose error names the fix, then a test, then docs last.

Every text needs the Reply or Document rules and the catalog of AI tells. Only docs, PR text, and commit text need the Diátaxis, Google style, and Global English lines. writing-for-agents' branch test puts what every branch needs in the main file and the rest behind a pointer.

state.title: Can the grill close with no change, so that the shared understanding is the result?
state.description:
The glossary gives the grill two paths when it closes: a change that fits one session goes to implement, and a bigger change goes through to-spec and to-tickets. It has no path for a request whose result is an answer, such as an explanation or a diagnosis.

After Q3, the hosts for explain, how, why, and forensics must be Matt flow skills: grill-me, grill-with-docs, teach, implement, and the others that only the user starts. The grill is the likely host only if it can stop with no change. Today grill-me and grill-with-docs are one line each ('Run a /grilling session'), and grilling ends at its Shared understanding gate, so the Matt text already stops there. Only the glossary's path rule and ADR 0015 say that the grill goes on.
state.example:
/skill:grill-me why does the Update hold an item?
  grill: runs how and why as fact-finding
  grill: asks what the user wants to understand
  close: Shared understanding
  path: no change -> the flow ends here

options.label: Yes, a no-change path
options.does: The grill's path rule gets a third path: no change, and the flow ends at the shared understanding. The glossary and ADR 0015 say so.

options.label: No, the grill always leads to a change
options.does: Every grill ends in implement or in to-spec and to-tickets. A request that ends in an answer needs teach or another host, or its Addon leaves vstack.

state.title: Which ways to move a floating pane do you want?
state.description:
In Zellij you move a floating pane with the keys of move mode, resize it with the keys of resize mode, and drag it with the mouse to any spot.

The plugin can do the keys fully: it keeps a position and a size per float and writes them into the CSS. The mouse is different. Tern ends every drag in a corner of the tab, and it tells a plugin nothing about where the pointer went. So a drag to any spot needs a change in Tern itself.

Every later question builds on this one.

options.label: Keys only
options.does: Ctrl+G M with H, J, K or L moves the focused float a step. Ctrl+G R with H, J, K or L makes it narrower, wider, shorter or taller. The mouse still cannot move a float.

options.label: Keys, plus a drag that lands in a corner
options.does: As A, and a float that you drag leaves the cascade and sits in the corner where Tern drops it, at Tern's own size.

options.label: Keys now, and ask Tern for free placement
options.does: As A, and you file an issue on stencil-hq/tern-sdk that asks for a float position that a plugin can set and read, or a drag that stays where you let go.

- 13 fit "picked only inside a Matt skill" as they are. 8 fit with a scope fix in their text or judge question (for example fix-root-causes says fix every matching instance; sequence-verifiable-units forces trunk rebasing).
- 2 lose meaning outside Matt work: encode-lessons-in-structure (captures every correction in any session) and guard-the-context-window (large reads in plain chat).
- Several overlap Matt text: test-behavior-not-implementation with tdd, fix-root-causes with diagnosing-bugs, exhaust-the-design-space with prototype and DESIGN-IT-TWICE.

19 principles are adopt items. A scope fix in a principle's text flips it to adapt; a fix in its judge question does not.

- grill-with-docs: which cases to ask, and which facts to look up first.
- to-spec: what an Update spec must contain.
- to-tickets: how to slice an Update.
- implement: which scripts and gates to run (plan, merge, prepare, gates, check-register, load smoke, jev sample prompts).

to-spec and to-tickets synthesize from the conversation, so the grill's knowledge already reaches them.

state.title: Ship the simple-english change as described?
state.description:
Before: The Document rules set hard limits. A sentence stops at 20 or 25 words, a heading needs three sentences under it, a list needs three items, and a paragraph stops at six sentences. check, verify, config, and settings become `make sure that` and `configuration`. may, might, could, should, and would are all banned. The Reply rules ban headers, lists, bold, and tables, and the self-check deletes every `#` and `-` line.

After: The 20-word and 25-word limits are targets, and the writer splits a sentence that needs a second read. A heading, a list, or a table is allowed when it carries structure, with no minimum. A document picks one word per concept and keeps it. should and would stay banned. may, might, and could are allowed only for a fact that the writer is not sure of. The Reply rules say that the Document rules do not apply to chat, allow a list, a table, a heading, or a code block that carries structure, and add the modal rule. CHECK mode still reports against the full standard in the rule catalog, and the skill now says that the catalog is stricter than Plain mode. In `references/use-cases.md`, the runbook and commit limits become targets.

Who sees it: you, in every chat reply, `ask` question, page, PR, and commit, because the vstack-prose rule loads this skill in every agent. The description changed, but the skill is hidden, so no request selects it. The run raises the patch version to 0.1.54.

state.title: What makes a skill standalone rather than an Addon?
state.description:
Your correction: not every non-Matt skill is an Addon. unslop, simple-english, and good-css can be standalone skills. Session 1 defined an Addon as every skill that is not a Matt skill, so the glossary, ADR 0015, and the settled ticket need a third kind and a test for it.

What the three have in common: each applies to the output of any task (text or a figure), not to one kind of work such as an Update. Each comes from its own Upstream or from pstack, not from a vstack workflow. Today good-css is model-invoked, unslop and simple-english are manual-only, and the always-on vstack-prose rule loads unslop and simple-english for every text.

options.does: A standalone skill sets how any output looks or reads (writing, figures, styles), whatever the work is. It can start anywhere: by its description, by a rule, or by name.

options.label: A fixed list
options.does: Standalone skills are a list in the glossary and the register. No general test.

Parentheses are allowed for a short definition, an example, or an aside. Bold stays banned, and simple-english still wins where it differs from unslop.

state.title: Ship the skill-creator change as described?
state.description:
Before: for a vstack target, skill-creator ran the hand-edit steps itself. It made a branch, a patch version bump, a CHANGELOG entry, the register check, and a PR. It refused a vstack adopt item and stopped.

After: outside a vstack-edit run, skill-creator hands every vstack target to `skill://vstack-edit` before it writes anything, whatever the Disposition. A vstack target is a new skill in vstack, or a skill whose real path is in a vstack clone's `plugin/`. Inside an active vstack-edit run, skill-creator writes only the draft in the run's worktree and does not hand the work back. Step 5 no longer tells it to run check-register, because the vstack-edit gates run it.

Who sees the difference: the user, whose request such as "add a skill to vstack" now goes through the vstack-edit flow, and who can now change an adopt item after the flip question. The agent that loads skill-creator sees the new branch. The callers ask-vstack, session-lessons, and vstack-edit need no change. vstack-edit step 4 already says that skill-creator writes only the draft in its run.

All three reviewers found nothing. This run itself used the new rule: the draft step used skill-creator once, and it started no second vstack-edit run.

options.does: Let both groups reach the same gateway.

state.title: What connections will change when we remove the shared backend?
state.description: Today the web app and mobile app both call one backend, which calls billing and search. After the change, each app calls a dedicated backend and both backends use the same billing service. We need to account for each connection added, removed, or retained.

options.label: Split backends
options.does: Give each client its own backend.

options.label: Keep shared
options.does: Retain the current connections.

state.title: Which old systems must we replace first?
state.description: Sales keeps leads in a desktop database and copies orders into spreadsheets. Finance rekeys those orders into an aging accounting package, while support uses a separate ticket tool. We need a record of the systems each department uses today before choosing a replacement.

options.label: Orders first
options.does: Replace the spreadsheets and order rekeying first.

options.label: Support first
options.does: Replace the ticket tool first.

state.title: When can a refund be approved without a person?
state.description: If the order is older than 30 days, reject the request. Otherwise check whether the amount exceeds $100, then check whether the account has a prior refund. The outcome of each check determines the next check or the final decision.

options.label: Strict checks
options.does: Require a person for large amounts or prior refunds.

options.label: Amount only
options.does: Require a person only for large amounts.

state.title: When must checkout confirm payment to the customer?
state.description: The browser sends an order to checkout, checkout asks the bank to reserve funds, and the bank returns a receipt. Checkout then writes the order and replies to the browser. The decision is whether that reply occurs before or after the bank sends its final confirmation.

options.label: Wait for bank
options.does: Reply only after final confirmation arrives.

options.label: Reply early
options.does: Reply after the reservation receipt arrives.

state.title: Can a paused export resume after its credentials expire?
state.description: An export can be queued, running, paused, completed, or cancelled. A user can pause a running export and resume a paused one only while credentials remain valid. We need to decide what happens when credentials expire during the pause.

options.label: Require renewal
options.does: Keep the export paused until credentials are renewed.

options.label: Cancel export
options.does: Move the export to cancelled when credentials expire.

state.title: Can one project belong to more than one workspace?
state.description: A workspace has a name and an owner, and a project has a name and a creation date. Users join workspaces through memberships that carry a role. We need to decide whether a project belongs to one workspace or can belong to several, without choosing storage details.

options.label: One workspace
options.does: Give each project one workspace owner.

options.label: Several workspaces
options.does: Allow several workspaces to share a project.

state.title: When will we announce the shutdown to customers?
state.description: The contract ends on June 30, the export tool becomes available on May 1, and the last renewal occurs on May 15. The announcement can happen on April 1 or May 1. We need to compare the order and spacing of these dated events.

options.label: April notice
options.does: Announce one month before exports open.

options.label: May notice
options.does: Announce when exports open.

state.title: Who must hand off an enterprise order to finance?
state.description: Sales negotiates the order, legal reviews the contract, finance checks credit, and operations provisions the account. A rejected credit check sends the order back to sales. We need to see which team owns each task and where responsibility changes hands.

options.label: Sales owns handoff
options.does: Sales sends the signed contract to finance.

options.label: Legal owns handoff
options.does: Legal sends the approved contract to finance.

state.title: Which product fixes belong in the next sprint?
state.description: We rate six fixes by customer impact and engineering effort. The login fix has high impact and low effort, while the reporting rewrite has high impact and high effort. We need to place all fixes against those two measures before choosing a priority rule.

options.label: Fast gains
options.does: Prioritize high impact with low effort.

options.label: Big investments
options.does: Prioritize the highest impact regardless of effort.

state.title: Which vendor has the most balanced fit for our team?
state.description: We score three vendors from 1 to 10 on reliability, cost, support, flexibility, and setup speed. One vendor wins on cost but loses on support, while another has moderate scores everywhere. We need to compare the shape of each vendor’s strengths across all five measures.

options.label: Balanced fit
options.does: Choose the vendor with no weak score.

options.label: Specialist fit
options.does: Choose the vendor with the strongest reliability score.

state.title: Which daily support hours need extra staff?
state.description: We have one average ticket count for each hour of the day, from midnight through the next midnight. Demand peaks near 23:00 and 01:00, so the first and last hours are adjacent in the daily cycle. We need to compare the magnitude of demand around that repeating cycle.

options.label: Night coverage
options.does: Add staff around midnight.

options.label: Day coverage
options.does: Add staff during the largest daytime peak.

state.title: Will community answers reduce support work over time?
state.description: A solved ticket adds an answer to a shared knowledge base. More answers help customers solve problems themselves, and their feedback improves the stored answers. Better answers attract more readers, whose new questions lead to more solved tickets and added knowledge.

options.label: Invest in answers
options.does: Use support time to grow and improve the shared knowledge base.

options.label: Ticket only
options.does: Close tickets without adding shared answers.

state.title: Where must a workspace setting apply?
state.description: The company account contains regions, each region contains workspaces, and each workspace contains projects. A restriction at any scope applies to everything inside it. We need to compare a company-wide restriction with one that applies only inside a single workspace.

options.label: Company scope
options.does: Apply the restriction to every region and workspace.

options.label: Workspace scope
options.does: Apply the restriction only within the chosen workspace.

state.title: How far must we break down the import work?
state.description: The import feature divides into parsing, validation, and saving. Parsing divides into CSV and JSON readers, while validation divides into required fields and duplicate checks. Every smaller item belongs to exactly one larger item.

options.label: Detailed ownership
options.does: Assign an owner to each smallest item.

options.label: Broad ownership
options.does: Assign an owner only to parsing, validation, and saving.

state.title: Who can escalate an incident to the executive team?
state.description: Two on-call engineers report to the platform lead, who reports to the engineering director. The customer support lead reports to the operations director. We need to decide who receives escalations and which reporting relationships carry them upward.

options.label: Platform route
options.does: Send technical escalations through the platform lead.

options.label: Incident lead
options.does: Give one incident lead authority to reach both directors.

state.title: At which level must we enforce tenant isolation?
state.description: The product has user-facing screens above business rules, data access, and storage. Each level uses the services below it and hides those details from the level above. We need to compare enforcing isolation in business rules with enforcing it in storage.

options.label: Business rules
options.does: Check tenant boundaries in the business rules.

options.label: Storage rules
options.does: Check tenant boundaries in the storage system.

state.title: Can a technician replace the sensor without removing the circuit board?
state.description: Our field device contains a lid, a seal, a circuit board, a sensor, and a base. These parts sit one above another along the assembly direction, and the sensor connector sits below the board. We need to inspect how the parts fit together and which parts must come off first.

options.label: Top access
options.does: Move the connector so the sensor can lift out after the lid.

options.label: Keep assembly
options.does: Require board removal before sensor replacement.

state.title: Where will the new testing benches fit in the office?
state.description: The lab shares one floor with a meeting room, a storage room, and the engineering desks. The lab needs two benches, clear walking space, and access to the door and power outlets. We need to inspect the room arrangement and furniture positions on that floor.

options.label: Expand lab
options.does: Move the storage room wall to make room for two benches.

options.label: Use desk space
options.does: Place one bench beside the engineering desks.

state.title: Which customers qualify for the beta?
state.description: Some customers use the mobile app, some pay for the team plan, and some enabled audit logs. A customer can belong to any combination of those groups. We need to compare inviting customers in all three groups with inviting anyone in at least two.

options.label: All three
options.does: Invite only customers who meet every condition.

options.label: Any two
options.does: Invite customers who meet at least two conditions.

state.title: At which signup step are we losing most prospects?
state.description: Last month 10,000 people visited signup, 4,000 started an account, 1,200 verified email, and 300 invited a teammate. Each later group is a subset of the previous group. We need to compare the drop in people at each step before choosing an intervention.

options.label: Email fix
options.does: Improve email verification.

options.label: Invite fix
options.does: Improve the teammate invitation step.

state.title: Which support category needs another specialist?
state.description: Last week billing received 240 tickets, login received 160, exports received 90, and integrations received 310. We need to compare totals across these four categories. The choice is whether to staff the largest category or the one with the longest average handling time.

options.label: Volume first
options.does: Add a specialist to integrations.

options.label: Handling time first
options.does: Add a specialist to the category with the longest handling time.

state.title: How will next quarter’s cloud bill reach the target?
state.description: The current monthly bill is $80,000. New customers add $15,000, storage cleanup removes $8,000, reserved capacity removes $12,000, and a new region adds $5,000. We need to account for each increase and decrease between the starting bill and the proposed final bill.

options.label: Use reservations
options.does: Include the $12,000 saving from reserved capacity.

options.label: Stay flexible
options.does: Keep on-demand capacity and omit that saving.

state.title: Which parts of storage consume most of our budget?
state.description: The $100,000 storage budget divides into customer data, backups, and logs. Customer data divides further into images, videos, and documents, with videos consuming $55,000 of the total. We need to compare the relative sizes of these nested spending shares.

options.label: Video cleanup
options.does: Reduce the largest share by deleting unused videos.

options.label: Broad cleanup
options.does: Reduce spending across every category.

state.title: Which region and service combinations need attention?
state.description: We measured error rates for four services in each of five regions. Payments in Europe has an 8% error rate, while most other service and region pairs are below 1%. We need to compare every pair and spot clusters of high values.

options.label: Regional fix
options.does: Focus on all services in the worst region.

options.label: Service fix
options.does: Focus on the worst service across regions.

state.title: When did the new cache start reducing latency?
state.description: We recorded median request latency every hour for two weeks. We enabled the new cache halfway through the period, and latency declined over the following three days. We need to compare the continuous change before and after that date.

options.label: Keep cache
options.does: Retain the cache if the decline continues.

options.label: Roll back
options.does: Remove the cache if latency returns to its prior level.

state.title: Can the migration finish before the launch date?
state.description: Data cleanup runs July 1 through July 10, backfill runs July 8 through July 20, and validation runs July 21 through July 25. The launch is July 26, and validation cannot start until backfill ends. We need to compare task durations, overlap, and the dependency on finishing backfill.

options.label: Overlap work
options.does: Start backfill while cleanup is still running.

options.label: Serial work
options.does: Wait until cleanup ends before starting backfill.

state.title: Does a larger account take longer to onboard?
state.description: For each of 80 customer accounts, we recorded employee count and days needed to finish onboarding. Some small accounts took weeks, while some large accounts finished in days. We need to inspect whether these two measured variables move together and which accounts are unusual.

options.label: Size-based help
options.does: Assign extra onboarding help to larger accounts.

options.label: Case-based help
options.does: Assign help based on delays rather than company size.

state.title: Will the analytics platform fit in one shared cluster?
state.description: Events enter collectors, pass through stream processing, land in object storage, and reach a query engine and dashboards. All of these services run as containers in a Kubernetes cluster with shared monitoring and scheduling. We need to see the whole path and the cluster services that support it.

options.label: Shared cluster
options.does: Run ingestion, storage access, and queries in one cluster.

options.label: Separate queries
options.does: Move the query services to another cluster.

state.title: When must a reviewer approve a research summary?
state.description: A researcher collects interview notes, an analyst turns them into findings, a reviewer checks the evidence, and a product manager publishes the summary. Each person passes a specific document to the next person. We need to compare approval before the findings become a draft with approval just before publication.

options.label: Review findings
options.does: Check the findings before the analyst writes the summary.

options.label: Review draft
options.does: Check the finished summary before publication.

state.title: Which data can analysts use without an engineer’s approval?
state.description: We keep untouched source records, cleaned records with validated fields, and curated totals that are ready for reports. Each storage tier has a different quality guarantee and access rule. We need to decide whether analysts can read cleaned records or only curated totals.

options.label: Cleaned access
options.does: Let analysts read validated records and curated totals.

options.label: Curated only
options.does: Limit analysts to report-ready totals.

state.title: Who owns each step that turns customer feedback into training data?
state.description: Support supplies raw feedback, analysts remove personal details, reviewers approve labels, and machine learning engineers publish a training set. The data changes form at every step. We need to show the data entering and leaving each step alongside the role allowed to perform it.

options.label: Analyst ownership
options.does: Let analysts remove details and propose labels.

options.label: Reviewer ownership
options.does: Let reviewers remove details and approve labels.

state.title: Which systems can connect directly to the reporting platform?
state.description: The CRM, billing service, and product events feed one central data platform. That platform serves dashboards, a finance export, and a partner API. We need to compare the source and consumer connections, including whether the partner can bypass the central platform.

options.label: Central access
options.does: Require every consumer to use the central platform.

options.label: Direct partner
options.does: Let the partner read directly from billing.

state.title: Which access rights will contractors receive?
state.description: We have engineers, analysts, contractors, and administrators, plus ingestion, storage, query, and export components. Each role can have no access, read access, or write access to each component. We need to compare these permissions for every role and component pair.

options.label: Read only
options.does: Give contractors read access to queries and no export access.

options.label: Read and export
options.does: Give contractors read access to queries and exports.

state.title: Where do paid trial users go after the trial ends?
state.description: Of 1,000 trial users, 600 enter self-service sales and 400 enter assisted sales. Self-service sends 180 users to paid plans and 420 to churn, while assisted sales sends 220 to paid plans and 180 to churn. We need to preserve the user counts as each group splits and the paid groups combine.

options.label: More assistance
options.does: Move 100 trial users from self-service to assisted sales.

options.label: Self-service fix
options.does: Keep the split and improve self-service conversion.

state.title: Which causes of failed releases must we address first?
state.description: Failed releases share one observed outcome, an incomplete database migration. Candidate causes fall under people, tooling, procedure, and environment, with missing reviews under people and stale credentials under environment. We need to group the possible causes under those categories before choosing an action.

options.label: Procedure first
options.does: Add a migration review and rehearsal.

options.label: Tooling first
options.does: Fix migration checks and credential handling.

state.title: Which parts of our search product must we build rather than buy?
state.description: Customers need relevant results, which depend on ranking, indexing, compute, and storage. Ranking is novel and changing fast, indexing is a common packaged service, and compute and storage are standardized utilities. We need to compare closeness to customer value with how mature each capability is.

options.label: Build ranking
options.does: Keep novel ranking in-house and buy mature capabilities.

options.label: Build all
options.does: Keep ranking, indexing, compute, and storage in-house.

state.title: Can we start another feature while reviews are blocked?
state.description: Our team has work waiting, in progress, in review, and finished. The in-progress limit is three items and the review limit is two, but both review items are blocked on legal approval. We need to inspect the current items, their status, and capacity limits before pulling new work.

options.label: Stop starting
options.does: Clear blocked reviews before starting another item.

options.label: Start another
options.does: Use an empty in-progress slot for new work.

state.title: Where does a first-time administrator need more help?
state.description: A new administrator discovers the product, signs up, invites staff, and runs the first report. Interviews show curiosity at discovery, confidence after signup, frustration during invitations, and relief after the report. We need to follow this person’s actions and feelings through the experience.

options.label: Invitation help
options.does: Add guided help during staff invitations.

options.label: Report help
options.does: Add guided help before the first report.

state.title: Must the customer see the identity check before delivery?
state.description: The customer places an order, sees a confirmation, tracks shipment, and accepts delivery. Behind those visible steps, staff check identity, reserve stock, and arrange transport with a partner. We need to compare what the customer sees with the hidden work that supports each stage.

options.label: Visible check
options.does: Ask the customer to complete the identity check after ordering.

options.label: Hidden check
options.does: Let staff complete the check without a customer-facing step.

state.title: Where will the production workers run?
state.description: The web artifact runs on two hosts in the public zone on port 443. Three worker replicas run on private hosts and reach a database host on port 5432. We need to compare the exact zones, machines, artifacts, and ports when workers move to a second region.

options.label: Second region
options.does: Place two worker replicas on private hosts in the second region.

options.label: Single region
options.does: Keep every worker replica on the current private hosts.

state.title: What must change before we can remove the shared package?
state.description: Checkout and billing both depend on the pricing package, which depends on currency utilities. Currency utilities also depend on pricing for formatting rules, so those packages require each other. We need to inspect shared prerequisites and this circular requirement before removing pricing.

options.label: Break circle
options.does: Move formatting rules out of currency utilities first.

options.label: Keep package
options.does: Retain pricing until both consumers migrate.

state.title: How must the new payment handlers share behavior?
state.description: CardPayment and BankPayment both inherit validation and submit operations from Payment. A Payment owns several Refund objects, each with amount and status, and can call refund(). We need to compare inheritance with a handler that delegates to an owned Payment object.

options.label: Inherit behavior
options.does: Make each payment handler inherit from Payment.

options.label: Delegate behavior
options.does: Make each payment handler own a Payment object.

state.title: What belongs in the first release of team onboarding?
state.description: An administrator creates a workspace, invites members, assigns roles, and checks activity. Under each activity we have small user tasks, such as bulk invitations and custom roles. We need to separate tasks needed for a complete first experience from tasks reserved for later releases.

options.label: Thin first release
options.does: Include one basic task under every activity.

options.label: Deep invitations
options.does: Ship advanced invitation tasks before custom roles and activity checks.

state.title: Which constraints must the orders database enforce?
state.description: The orders table has a UUID primary key, a non-null customer_id, and a NUMERIC(12,2) total with a nonnegative check. customer_id references customers.id, and an index covers customer_id plus created_at. We need to decide whether deleting a customer rejects the deletion or cascades to its orders.

options.label: Reject deletion
options.does: Use a foreign key that prevents deletion of referenced customers.

options.label: Cascade deletion
options.does: Use a foreign key that deletes related orders.
